utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today, Thursday, the 11th of March, 2010, I'd like to greet General Petkovic, our witness, the accused, the Defence teams, Mr. Scott, his collaborators, and everyone else assisting us. I will now hand down an oral decision concerning the Petkovic Defence's request for a statement of reasons in writing, or, in the alternative, a certification of appeal of the oral decision of the 10th of March, 2010. At the hearing held on the 10th of March, 2010, the Petkovic Defence requested that the Chamber provide additional grounds for its oral decision of the 10th of March, 2010, concerning the allocation of two additional hours for the additional examination of Milivoj Petkovic or, in the alternative, it requested that the Chamber certify the appeal that it intends to file against the said oral decision. The Chamber notes that the request for a statement of reasons -- an additional statement of reasons for the oral decision of the 10th of March, 2010, has no grounds, as the decision in question has been duly justified. With regard to the request for certification of appeal against the oral decision, the Chamber notes that the Petkovic Defence has failed to provide reasons for its request, in the light of the conditions of Rule 73(B). As a result, the Chamber hereby dismisses the request. Concerning General Petkovic's testimony now, I believe that 54 minutes remain for Ms. Alaburic, if I'm not mistaken. You have the floor, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and to you, General, and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, a few questions to start off with with respect to the cross-examination conducted by my learned friend Mr. Scott dealing with the co-operation between the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska. And this topic was dealt with on pages 50564 of the transcript. And, among others, Mr. Scott asked you the following: Did the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska conduct joint combat operations against the Muslims? Do you remember that part of the examination, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One of the documents that Mr. Scott put to you was document number P1643. General, we can use e-court. It will make it faster. It was a report by Ivo Lozancic from Zepce, dated the 10th of March, 1993, sent to Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Bruno Stojic. And Mr. Scott focused on the following sentence: "It is necessary to open negotiations with the third party as a possibility of resolving the question for us and Usora." Now, I had the impression, General, that you wished to explain the context in which that was written, and that you also wanted to tell us whether it had anything to do with individual joint operations manned by the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska against the Muslims. Tell us now.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no joint combat. These areas were under a total siege and you couldn't reach them. Zepce was the furthest, and from the south side it was blocked by Zenica, Veliko Srediste, and a large number of units, and Zepce and Usora had no contact with any HVO unit. We could not access it, we couldn't get within reach of 100 kilometres, because the BH Army was around about. So that was one of the most difficult problems to resolve, Zepce being left as one of the most difficult enclaves of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, 4D566 is the next document I'd like us to look at, and it's the map which you, yourself, prepared showing the situation on the territory of Central Bosnia and part of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone. So let's have a look where Zepce is, exactly, and what it is you were talking about. That's the map. Tell us, please, General, does Zepce border on territory controlled by the Serbs, in part?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does border on that to the west, that is to say, north of Zenica, which is where the Serbs were in contact with part of the Zepce municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, according to your estimation, this Croatian enclave, could it have survived had it not had the possibility of communicating with the outside world through the territory under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have survived, no chance whatsoever of it surviving.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document that you were shown by Mr. Scott in this context is document P2931, which is an order of yours, General, sent to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade and Rama Brigade and to Mr. Siljeg in Prozor. And in item 3 of that order, which was sent on the 24th of June, 1993, you state: "I forbid support to our present [as interpreted] allies." And then in point 4, you say: "Provide support to the new allies." So you're withholding it from the old allies and provide support to the new allies. Tell us, General, the former allies, that is to say, up until this order was issued on the 23rd of June, 1993, who were those former allies?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was figuratively stated. They were members of the BH Army who, up until that date, had taken control of Travnik, expelled the Croats, taken Kakanj, expelled the Croats from Kakanj. Those were the former allies. And these new ones, new allies, were those who took over the Croats on their own territory and succeeded in organising them and transporting the civilian population, in part, to the Republic of Croatia and through Kupres to Livno. That's what that was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, you've already told us this, but you can remind us, when, in your opinion, did an all-out, total war begin between the HVO and BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, total war began in June, to all intents and purposes, and it reached a peak on the 30th of June, because it was in June that Travnik was attacked, taken control of, Croats expelled, Kakanj continued, Fojnica continued, and further on, so the whole of Bosnia and the whole of the HVO in Bosnia was totally blocked and being attacked from all sides, and we had no prospects at all. And that is why we had 5.000 dead -- 5.000 dead in the clashes -- well, if we call them former allies up until then of the BH Army, members of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next topic, General, re-subordination. My question to you is this: Is there any automatic re-subordination? For example, Tuta, with 50 members of the Convicts Battalion, comes into the territory of Gornji Vakuf, so does that mean that he is automatically re-subordinated to Zrinko Tokic, who was the commander of the brigade in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not unless Tuta had been sent by somebody and an order written that he was being re-subordinated. He could come there and say, I am re-subordinating myself. So for re-subordination, there must be the proper documentation to back that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned and said that Tuta, as a unit being re-subordinated possibly, must have been informed about that. Now, what about the brigade commander; would he have to have been informed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. He has to know who he was getting, and somebody getting into the area can only work on his own bat if they're not re-subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next topic is this: Mr. Scott, on page 50683 of the transcript, mentioned several of your agreements and the permission you gave for labour on the part of detainees, and he said that that permission was given following your order of the 14th of October, 1993. So let's look at that order now of the 14th of October, 1993. The number of the document is P5873. Tell us, General, how come you issued this order in the first place? Can you explain the circumstances of that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on that day I received a delegation from the International Red Cross Committee because we were supposed to decide about the holding of two meetings, one in Tomislavgrad and the other in Mostar, which would involve about 100 officers and NCOs, and the ICRC would talk about International Humanitarian Law. And that was arranged, and the people from the ICRC spent two days in Mostar on both sides, both banks. And they went with me -- they came to me to talk to me, and they said that they had been to the east bank, and asked them there to regulate questions of human labour. And then they told me that it would be a good idea if I were to issue an order, and that's what I did. That's how I drafted the order forbidding any more such people to be taken for that purpose, and, if necessary, then the Main Staff would make the decision and it would be far off from the front-line so as not to bring anybody into jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at P7075, the next order. Well, I apologise, it's not an order; it's actually a document. It's a document dated the 18th of December, 1993, signed by the then assistant minister of defence, Marijan Biskic. And towards the end of that document, it says that: "I forbid, without permission from the Security Sector, the taking out of prisoners for labour." Now, my question to you, General, is this: From that time on, the Security Sector, did it issue permission for prisoners to be taken out for labour?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Sector took it upon themselves to supervise and see where the people were being taken -- prisoners were being taken out for labour or not. And as far as I remember, they gave permission for some people to go out to work in certain localities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next topic, let's move on: The military disciplinary courts. The page of the transcript is 50283. Tell us, please, General, the legal system in Herceg-Bosna, with respect to the new provisions, was it similar to the system applied in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was mostly similar, and all the documents and material was used, the documents issued in the Republic of Croatia, to be adapted or copied out for other purposes -- these other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at 4D1331, the next document, 4D331 [as interpreted]. It's a decision on establishing military disciplinary courts. It's the 14th of November. Franjo Tudjman took the decision. It has to do with the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Army. Tell me, did Mate Boban ever issue a decision or a similar one in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never issued a decision on establishing military disciplinary courts. And the year is 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now for the following subject. On transcript page 50077 and 50078, the Stojic Defence showed you document 4D348. This is a report from Mr. Miro Andric compiled on the 27th of January, 1993. General, can you confirm the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Andric compiled this document. It's authentic, and all the people mentioned under 1 to 5 were with him in Gornji Vakuf; in fact, in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you read this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, does it correctly depict the situation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Andric described all the events from the 12th of January. He described all his meetings, everything that was going on until he left the area of Gornji Vakuf or, rather, until the time that he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On page 50326 of the transcript, 50326, Judge Antonetti asked you how it is that the Defence Department was an administrative organ that had the Main Staff as one of its components, which was an operative organ. General, my question is: Is the Defence Department, as you understand it, just an administrative body?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have a look at it as a whole, if you have a look at the Main Staff within the framework of the Defence Department, then it's an administrative and an operative organ, because you can't exclude the Main Staff from that body.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On page 50098 of the transcript to 50133, you were asked about assistant commanders of operative zones and brigades and battalions, for the medical corps, security, and for information and propaganda. My question is: Who appointed these assistant commanders -- these deputy commanders, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had to be appointed within the chain of command by the highest-ranking levels of the Defence Department, by the body responsible for appointing such people. They made such suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's have a look at 2D567. This is a decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department, dated the 17th of October, 1992. I'll go through certain provisions very quickly. In item 4, it says that deputy commanders for security in the commands of operative zones shall be appointed by the representative of the Defence Department, as suggested by the deputy commander for security, and also deputy commanders for brigades. Item 5, this also concerns the health sector, the chief of the medical corps in the brigades shall be appointed by representatives of the Defence Department. Then we have the Sector for Morale. That's item 6 of the document. And for the Sector for Morale, apart from deputy commanders, it also says that all other officials and operative officers in the Sector for Morale shall be appointed by the deputy representative for morale, with the acceptance of the head of the Defence Department or someone authorised by that person. General, as far as you remember, was that the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was how one had to proceed. These are the provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at P601, General. This is a programme of work for the Sector for Morale for 1992. It's dated the 19th of October, 1992. The programme was established by the assistant for the Defence Department then, Mr. Bozo Rajic. In the document, there are a number of important items. It's already an exhibit. I'll just draw your attention to one part of the document towards the end of the introductory part, before the numbers 1, 2, 3 on the next page in the Croatian version. I think it's the same in the English version. In that part, it says that they suggest -- the authority for appointing all officials shall be the authority of this sector, and you can influence -- they can influence the officials appointed. Subordination and control shall also be established, because "appointment" also means the right to dismiss certain employees, and so on. General, did you know that the initiative for this decision came from the Sector for Morale, itself?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They followed the usual guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on to the next subject. General, General Praljak asked you questions about combat and non-combat components of the military structure; page 50186 of the transcript to 50190. Amongst non-combat components of the military structure, you included the military police. My question is whether all units and services of the military police are part of the non-military -- the non-combat, correction, component of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police, amongst its tasks -- well, didn't mention that the military police was a combat unit, but at certain periods of time there were certain tasks, so to speak, where parts of the military police were declared to be combat components, but the tasks never actually stated that the military police had to perform combat operations. After a certain amount of time, there would be certain changes within the structure, and then the possibility would be given, through orders and through other documents, for part of the police to be used in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Coric Defence, on pages 50223 to 5, showed you P960, document P960. These are instructions from Mr. Bruno Stojic on implementing the reorganisation of the military police units. The date is the 28th of December, 1992. And now for the following document, and then I will put my question. Have a look at document P957. This is a decision on the structure of the military police of the HVO. The date is the 26th of December, two days earlier. It was taken by Mr. Coric and Mr. Stojic on that date. General, my question is: As Chief of the Main Staff, did you or anyone else from the Main Staff participate in this decision on the organisation of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we quite simply received this decision as a "fait accompli."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On page 50229 of the transcript, it says that you were shown a document, 5D5106, 5D5106. It's a decision on appointing a commander of a platoon of the brigade of military police in the Frankopan Brigade. The date is the 9th of April, 1993. Do you remember having seen this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at 4D2041 now. This is a decision from the military Police Administration, dated the 21st of August, 1993, in which one is reacting to the replacement of the commander of the Brigade police of the Knez Branimir Brigade in Citluk. It says: "Having examined order number 693, we are obliged to inform you of the following: "You do not have the authority to appoint and dismiss the brigade police commander. "2. If you believe that the brigade police commander is not performing his duty responsibly, you can request that the Military Police Administration of the HZ-HB relieve him of duty, providing the necessary explanation. "3. Should your request be approved, you will be able to propose a candidate for the new commander. "Send any remarks concerning the work of the brigade police to the Military Police Administration of the HVO." General, according to this document on the dismissal of the police commander of the Knez Branimir Brigade, who is responsible for appointing and dismissing brigade police commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the Administration of the Military Police. Everything else would be against the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On pages 50228 and 9 of the transcript, it says that you were shown your warning, P4262, P4262, your warning dated the 17th of August, 1993, on responsibility for command in the brigade military police. General, does this have the value of an order, this document of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. It was just a warning to prevent spreading blood amongst military police. This document that we saw previously was created three or four days after mine, so this is contrary to what I was claiming here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at P4922 now. This is an extract from instructions on the work of the brigade military police. It is -- it has the force of an order. On the 10th of September, 1993, it was issued by Mr. Valentin Coric. In that order, amongst other things -- well, I'll just mention a few items. It says military police platoons and brigades carry out the orders of the brigade commander within the framework of their responsibility. I'll skip another paragraph: "The HVO military police is a single body and is linked to battalions and companies under the command of the chief of the Military Police Administration. The structure of the military police in brigades is not permanent. Brigade platoons, within the framework of military police companies and battalions, can be used for general military and police affairs, under the command of the company commander, with the agreement of the brigade commander, and at that time their responsibilities towards the brigade shall cease." This extract from an obligation of a force of an order, as one says, was forwarded, as we can see, to all brigades. And it also says: "To military police platoons." That's handwritten. Was this extract also forwarded to the HVO Main Staff, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't forwarded to the HVO Main Staff, but this was also an attempt to normalise the relationship of the police within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On page 50225 to 31 of the transcript, it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With regard to the last document, Ms. Alaburic, could you tell us where you have the source to affirm that "10/09" is the 10th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, thank you for the question. I was expecting it. If you have a look at the second page of the Croatian version, you'll see that it was also forwarded to the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th Military Police Battalions. By the 1st of July, 1993 -- up to the 1st of July, 1993, there were five military police battalions, and in the second half of 1993, this was reorganised and there were eight military police battalions. So this document was forwarded to eight military police battalions, and as a result, the document is from 1993, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And probably I'm not 100 per cent sure. For 1994, Mr. Coric would not anymore be in the position as chief of the MPA?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Already in November 1993, Mr. Coric was no longer in that position, but I'm not talking about 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm just trying to exclude any possibilities that the document is from somewhere else, and that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, you have been shown P1099, 1099, which is a table showing the structure of the brigade. You were shown the first page of that document, General. It is a table, but not the actual formation of the brigades signed by Mr. Stojic. Tell me, General, was this table signed by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I can confirm whether it is a part of the whole. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, General. I'm just asking you whether he signed it.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Will you please find that document in our set of documents in the first binder. Please leaf through this document quickly and find where Bruno Stojic planned that the brigade military police would be part of the brigade structure. Can you do that quickly, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P1099. You can find it because the documents are in order. The question, General, is whether this diagram corresponds to the structure of the brigade passed by Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a schematic. It says here that it should be signed, though I can't see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Will you please find where it says that the brigade military police is part of the brigade structure?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it can't be found.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it indicated anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but then we have to look at all the appointments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it does not exist. Let us now look at document P957. We had it in our hands a moment ago. It is a decision by Mr. Bruno Stojic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes? THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I do apologise. Could you please ask the witness just one question: Whether all the brigades had the same structure? Counsel has just found one brigade formation, but all the brigades did not have the same structure. Thank you. If you could, Your Honours, please ask this of the witness. If not, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not possible for you, but it's an interesting question. We have an organigram, a typical organigram of a brigade. General Petkovic, did all the brigades have the same organigram or the same structure, or is this a special case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the exception may be as to whether brigade has two, three, or five battalions; that is, what differed one brigade from another. Some had two battalions. For example, Ante Starcevic had 1.300 men. It cannot have three. The Knez Domagoj at first had five battalions because it was numerically strong, and it may have had two independent companies. So the difference was in the number, and the greatest difference was the number of battalions that a brigade could form. And, secondly, another difference was whether the brigade had a sufficient number of artillery pieces or did it just have five mortars in a brigade, so you couldn't call it a division. The rest is more or less the same. So the main difference was the number of battalions. Depending on the strength of the brigade, the number of battalions was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, document P957. It's a decision on the structure of the HVO military police, which is from December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Ms. Alaburic, I apologise. Still talking about this document, P1099, when we look at the organigram that we have in front of us, I see in the first line, under the heading "Brigade Commander and Command," on the first line, I shall read, "Protection Platoon." What is the MP Platoon, what does it stand for? Witness, is that still the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Mindua, this a formation designed much earlier, so that if you have a military police platoon, you don't need a protective platoon. This was a structure that was set up at I don't know what level, and, as such, there is no need to have a protective platoon, because the need to protect the command will be done by the military police. So this was a structure from the very beginning. It was later revised, and many of these things were also revised later on. And what is shown with dotted lines, that was subject to changes; for instance, battalions and independent companies. And this depended on the possibilities regarding manpower in a particular municipality, whether they were sufficient or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I do have a request, if you could ask the witness a question. Since he is denying all the diagrams that are being shown, and in the last year we have seen some prepared here in The Hague, could you ask him whether he had an organigram of the Main Staff of the HVO of which he was the head? And if he did, let us see the position of the military police in the brigade. And an additional request: Why was this not called the NATO military police rather than the brigade military police? And I was a person who studied these matters at some length. Perhaps it would be better to call it the NATO military police rather than the brigade military police. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, due to the procedure, clearly, Mr. Coric could not ask this question later. He could ask another witness. But you were at the head of the HVO, and as he has already testified, he can't ask you any more questions. So I will take up this question, and could you answer it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honours. The Main Staff has its own structure which is prescribed, and, as such, it was adopted in September 1992. It was amended at the end of 1993, when General Roso took over as commander, perhaps two months after he took over. Up until then, it had an established structure. And we even saw lists of names of people who held certain positions. Therefore, the Main Staff did have its organisational structure and it had persons performing duties. You had the Witness Jasak, who pointed out his position on the diagram. A new change occurred at the end of 1993, when General Roso, Minister Jukic, and others came over. The Main Staff was reorganised, and the number of people in the Main Staff increased. So the Main Staff, of course, does have its structure, which we have seen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I did not find your answer to Mr. -- to my brother Mindua's question very, very clear. He pointed out that here we have an element, a protection platoon, and then there is also a platoon of military police. Now, you seem to be saying that all this is not really reliable, it changed over the course of time. That may well be so. I will, of course, not dispute this. The question is whether, then, it is convincing for the whole time that there is no place for military police in the structure of the battalion and whether what is here indicated by a platoon could not later on then be more important units of military police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one is denying that there was a military police in the brigade. This is the first scheme, designed at the beginning, and it was changed. This protection platoon was simply left out, was scrapped, because it was not necessary in the structure of the brigade. By a decision on the structure of the military police of the 26th of December, one can see that there are military police platoons that are attached to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the following documents we will be answering Your Honour Judge Trechsel, and we will be referring to all the points you have just raised, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about the structure of the Main Staff, tell us, who prescribed the structure of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence Department prescribed all the structures, including the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But "the Defence Department" doesn't mean anything, so tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the department, that is Mr. Stojic. No one else could sign them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you please wait for the translation, because you have been totally overlapping now. And this is addressed also to the witness. You -- as soon as the last word had left counsel's mouth, your mouth opened, and that's not the way that works. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us look at document P957 to see what was prescribed regarding brigade military police platoons. In the section relating to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Military Police Battalion, let us look at the text for the 2nd, which applies to all the battalions. It says: "The 2nd Battalion of the military police based in Tomislavgrad, covering the operational zone of North-Western Herzegovina." It consists of: The command, three companies, and six brigade platoons of military police. Tell us, General, according to this provision, what would you say? The military police platoon of the brigade, which does it belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belongs to the battalion of this operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look further down. As part of the battalion, there are six independent brigade platoons of the military police which are a component part of the brigade in the Operative Zone of North-Western Herzegovina. Tell us, please, General, this sentence, how do you interpret it? The platoons of the brigade military police, who do they belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belong to a certain battalion of the military police, be it the 2nd, 3rd, or 4th Battalion that we have come across here, or companies in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, then, how would you interpret the fact that it says that those platoons are also within the framework of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a single unified military police -- and they are, by assignment, attached to brigades. And then they become brigade military police, but they also belong to the military police battalion. This is a decision which is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the next document, P1707, 1707. This is a document of the head of the Military Police Administration, dated the 23rd of March, 1993, addressed to Bruno Stojic. It is a request for funds for the payment of salaries to the military police for February 1993. Under B, as we see in this document, there's mention of the brigade military police. And if we look at the table, we will see that Valentin Coric is seeking funds for the salaries of members of the brigade military police in the 3rd Battalion and the 4th Battalion of the Military Police. Tell me, General, on the basis of this document, to which entity the brigade military police belongs.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is to the 3rd and 4th Battalions of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Will we please look at the next document, which is P2020. This is, again, an order by Valentin Coric - I withdraw the word "again," from the 22nd of April, 1993. And in the second paragraph, Valentin Coric orders from members of the military police from the 2nd and 3rd Brigade, intervention groups should be formed which, together with the military police, that is, the Mostar Brigade of the Army of BiH, jointly patrol the town. What does it emerge from this order? Is Valentin Coric in charge of the brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is, because he says that the military police from the 2nd and 3rd Brigade should form intervention groups, together with the military police of the 1st Mostar Brigade of the ABiH, and that they should jointly patrol the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the document P2310. This is an information on a meeting that -- with Pero Markovic and the members of the civilian authorities of Capljina. A meeting was held with the representatives of military police, that is, representatives of the military police of the HVO, with the civilian authorities of Capljina municipality. And in the middle of the second page of the Croatian text, which is again the second page, paragraph 5, it is said as follows: "The first command of the brigade military police is given by the commander of the brigade, and it comes under the authority of the Administration of the Military Police, who reports on its work." Does this conclusion from the meeting agree with what you believe things should be like?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Petkovic, this was a bit a lump-sum question and answer. If I understand correctly, but I find it difficult to follow at that speed, I must admit, this could also be read as marking an exception. Normally, the MP of the brigade is under the authority of the commanders, and here it's excluded, and this might be an exception. What is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not an exception. The brigade will work on the affairs that the brigade commander received and issued, but it is duty-bound, in its work, to inform its superior organ, which is the military police battalion to which it belongs, in organisational terms; well, the police. But the battalion first is informed, and then it goes further on. It has to table a report on its work within the brigade to the superior organ of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. We have this on record. I'm sure we will have the occasion to go into this matter later also.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we can just clarify the beginning of the general's answer. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to go back a bit to the document presented by my learned colleague several minutes ago. It is document P01707, to make things proper. The first paragraph of that document, and she omitted to read a sentence from that, the sentence which says salaries were not calculated for military policemen in the brigade platoon of the Brigade of Knez Domagoj, the Bruno Busic Regiment, and the brigade platoons from the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina which were paid through those units. I just wanted to read that sentence out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, remind us of your answer. What was it that you said?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in certain areas, salaries were guaranteed for brigade platoons. Where it wasn't, then the military police asked the Defence Department to provide the salaries, because I know that individual municipalities paid soldiers and, by the same token, paid the military police in certain municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at P31 -- yes, my colleague Ms. Nozica has reminded me of a point. I wanted you to give me some explanation that -- you probably misspoke in line 8 of the previous page. When you started answering Judge Trechsel's question -- yes, I have very little time. That's why I'm speeding up, so I apologise to everybody. Judge Trechsel asked you about the brigade military police, and you said that the brigade will perform tasks pursuant to orders from the brigade commander. Did you mean the brigade or did you mean the brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant the brigade military police. It will perform its tasks in the brigade, but up the chain of command it must inform the military police what it was it did within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, do you in any way challenge the fact that the brigade military police performed the defined daily military police tasks and assignments pursuant to an order from the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not challenging that. That is what it did do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at document P3116, which is a report of the 4th Brigade Military Police. The commander is Ante Prlic, and it is a report dated the 2nd of July, 1993. And I'd like us to focus on the last sentence there, or the two last sentences, where it says the following: "Around Mostar, the brigade military police is on the alert and is in the police station, and is regularly implementing all the orders it receives from the brigade and the Military Police Administration. In the course of the past day, there were no problems." Tell us, General, a situation of this kind whereby orders are received both from the brigade commander and from the Military Police Administration, does that correspond to the actual situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one more document staying with that topic, and it is P5497. 5497 is the document number, which is a monthly report on the work of the 5th Battalion of the Military Police for the month of September 1993. And on the last page of that document, we have a review of the strength of the 5th Military Police Battalion, and mention made there is platoons in seven brigades and the brigade platoon in Konjic. Now, looking at this document, General, the brigade police, was it within the 5th Battalion of the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these platoons did come under the composition of the 5th Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What happened to the brigade military police when, at the head of the Ministry of Defence, we had Mr. Jukic, and in the Security Sector, Mr. Biskic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the general conclusion was about the institution of the brigade military police as it was organised hitherto, if you know? Was it given a positive assessment of its work or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the problems in the work of the brigade military police were reviewed, and so the new leadership decided to abolish the brigade military police forces in all the brigades and carried out a reorganisation of the overall military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, Judge Trechsel said, on page 50254 of the transcript -- he said: "We had the impression that the military police was integrated in the operative zone and that a command and order to the operative zone included everything that came under the operative zone commander, including the military police."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they do not have the exact words of Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of that, I'm going to quote the example of the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina in order to try and answer that question, and I hope, thereby, contribute to a clarification of the issue. Let's see what units existed in the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, to begin with, and to whom one of your orders sent to Miljenko Lasic for combat operations would refer. Tell us, in the territory of that operative zone, was the -- was there a special unit, Ludvig Pavlovic, and its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was headquartered in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That unit, was it directly subordinated to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the territory of that operative zone, did the 1st Light Assault Battalion of the Military Police have its headquarters too?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And to whom was the 1st Light Assault Battalion of the Military Police subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the territory of that same operative zone, did the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police have its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the territory of that same operative zone, did the brigades in municipalities incorporated by the operative zone have their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let's look at the situation. The commander of the operative zone was issued an order by you for some combat operation. You don't specify anything. It simply goes to the operative zone, to Miljenko Lasic personally. Now, tell us, an order of that kind, would it refer to the special Ludvig Pavlovic unit as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does the that order refer to the 1st Light Assault Brigade of the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that order refer to the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to correct the transcript in line 19. I was asking a hypothetical question, that General Petkovic, as Chief of the Main Staff, issues an order hypothetically to Miljenko Lasic, who was the commander of the North-East Herzegovina Operative Zone. So that was a hypothetical I was putting to the general, to avoid any misunderstanding. I think my time is almost up. May I know how many more minutes I have left, if any?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I give you a bit of time to reflect by putting a question to the witness. Mr. Petkovic, I find it difficult to understand how this -- militarily, how this works. We have a commander of the operation zone. In this operation, there are units which, you say, are not under his authority, and you give him the order to carry out an operation. Now, does the commander of the OZ have a possibility to somehow engage these elements or does he have to go to the Military Police Administration and consult with Mr. Coric, for instance, to say, Look, I would like to do this with this light assault unit; do you allow or could you order them? I would like to know how this works, because I cannot really imagine it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the units do not come within his composition, that is, the operative zone composition, he cannot issue them any assignments, regardless of the fact they had their headquarters in the same operative zone. They're not his units. What?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who's the "he"? Tell us who is the "he."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the operative zone. So he cannot issue an order for an assignment, just those who come down within the schematic of his units. Everything else, if necessary, he must ask me for -- about Ludvig Pavlovic and for the light assault battalion, to deploy that. So he doesn't have the right to deploy those forces. And today, in many armies throughout the world, you have within the territory of one area, a number of units which are not, organisationally speaking, linked to that particular commander. So if you want to deploy the unit, you have to ask permission, because he does not have authority over all the units located in a particular territory. So that's where the problem lies. So he has to ask the Main Staff for Ludvig Pavlovic, Bruno Busic, and so on. He can't deploy them himself, whereas they're very close by, they're in his vicinity. And also he can't deploy the light assault battalion, either, because he has to be given permission and approval to deploy those troops. He doesn't have the right, himself, to deploy such and such a unit, but he can ask for permission and he can be granted approval and permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you are saying that it is his initiative. He must analyse the order and then determine whether he wants to engage these additional forces that are within his zone, but not under his command, and then come back and ask for permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once he receives an order, it's his duty to assess what forces he has at his disposal, and then he says, I'm lacking something, I'm lacking Ludvig Pavlovic, for example, it would be a good thing if we had that. And then he will contact the Main Staff, explain why he needs the Ludvig Pavlovic, and will then ask for Ludvig Pavlovic. But the Chief of the Main Staff will have to assess the situation and, once again, whether to give him the whole unit, or 50 per cent of the men, or whatever. And the situation can be the reverse. If you give him such an order, then you can say, In addition to your unit, you have the right to deploy the Ludvig Pavlovic or whatever, the Bruno Busic, or anything else that the Main Staff has at its disposal. So he can be given permission for that, but mustn't take the men himself. If he's lacking in manpower, he has to ask for manpower and permission. So that's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This second scenario, that you, in giving an order, also, of course, make an analysis of the forces needed, and then directly on your initiative, also give the authority from the outset. But then still there is the issue of the military police unit, and wasn't it rather complicated and not very practical that the chief of the operations zone must then address himself to Mr. Coric to ask for permission to use this light assault unit if he thinks he needs it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, regardless of the fact that it's complicated, that's what he has to do. The deployment of the police in combat does not come within the remit and authority of the commander in the operative zone. So he has to ask permission if he's going to use the police in combat. And that's where his powers are limited. He doesn't have the right to take that decision himself. Once he's given permission, then he'll deploy that contingent for combat and will be responsible for it while he is using it. Otherwise, himself, he doesn't have the right to make this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's Mr. Coric on his feet. I wish to tell the Petkovic Defence that you have another six minutes left. Yes, Mr. Coric. Please do not forget that you will be testifying too, so we can come back to these points. What did you want to say? THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Your Honours, the same witness told us a few days ago, on the 9th of May in Mostar he enumerated all the units which took part in the operation of the 9th of May. He mentioned the military police, Bruno Busic, Ludvig Pavlovic, precisely the units that were there. And the witness said how it came about that this operation took place, so it would be realistic if we were to ask him now whether at the time this establishment of his, referring to the main task as presented by him, was it functioning that day, was it operative on that day? Did anybody ask the chief of the Military Police Administration whether the military police would be taking part? Let me just tell you the military police lost 12 of its men that day, and there were 40 wounded, on the 9th of May alone. So I'm going to ask him: At that time, did he or anybody else from that system, which was our system and establishment as well, any request to the military police, the Ludvig Pavlovic, which, as he said, on that day they took part in the combat and situation that took place. Let's be practical. Let's leave stories, as people recount them, apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, that will certainly be Mr. Coric's last question. With regard to the events of the 9th of May, I just discover that there were 12 MPs killed and 40 wounded. The combat was very intensive, it appears, given the figures that have been mentioned. The description of the 9th of May, does it tally with what you have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was an exceptional situation. When there was this emergency situation in Mostar, we are talking about a regular situation. For all other units, the commander of the operative zone deployed everybody he could to defend Mostar, and then the Main Staff was informed, and everything else. So this was an emergency situation that cropped up suddenly and we had to react. In Mostar, you had the military police at the time. To the south, in Heliodrom, you had the Bruno Busic and so on. But this was an emergency situation, and given this emergency situation, the commander of the operative zone took that step. And we were talking about procedure a moment ago, when you issue normal orders to the commander of the operative zone and tell him what he has to do and so on. But he could have given up, said, I don't have the authority, and allowed Mostar to fall into the hands of the BH Army. However, the forces and men he had in Mostar, he used to the last man, including the 1st Light Assault Battalion in certain sections in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, since Mr. Coric raised this subject, tell us, on the 9th of May, 1993, when you returned to Mostar, did you speak to Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met him in Mostar. We spoke to each other about everything that was happening in Mostar. And as far as I know, he spent the night in Mostar, that night in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My last question concerns a question put to you by Judge Trechsel again; paragraphs 76, 77, and 78 of the indictment. I have an overview of what I believe is relevant. Document 4D -- it's in English, 4D2034. It's in English, so don't look for it, General. General, Judge Trechsel asked you about those paragraphs. You started saying -- well, let me just point out that these are paragraphs in the indictment that concern Sovici and Doljani. I have, in fact, the Croatian text of the paragraphs. Could we please show the general this extract? Could the usher assist me so that the general can see what we are speaking about? General, you first mentioned a group of people who were in the school in Sovici, and together with their families, they were evacuated on the 5th of May, 1993. Judge Trechsel then said, No, that is not right. He mentioned the numbers mentioned in these paragraphs of the indictment; 70 to 90 military-aged Bosnian Muslim men. You then started answering on page 49505, and you said that they were members of the ABiH who had surrendered on the 17th, and they were provided with accommodation in the school, and on the 18th they were taken to the Ljubuski Prison. Judge Trechsel concluded his questions with the following words, I'll quote: [In English] "I am not quite convinced that we are talking about the same. But I will leave it at that, and if the Prosecution wants to take this up, I will let them. I just wanted to give you an opportunity to state your view. Thank you." [Interpretation] General, given that I would really like to assist in determining the truth in this case, you have these paragraphs from the indictment before you now. Could you please comment? And, Your Honours, in this document that I mentioned, 4D2034, I've also shown you some of the adjudicated facts that relate to these paragraphs of the indictment. We haven't dealt with this because we thought that this was indisputable. Paragraph 76, General, the Prosecution says that a certain number of Bosnian men tried -- or Muslim men tried to defend those villages. Were they civilians or were they members of a certain army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the 44th Brigade from Jablanica. The 4th Battalion was before Sovici, in front of Sovici. We saw a list of all the members of the 4th Battalion. We saw who had what sort of weapons. That's an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which army is concerned, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then the paragraph further says that late in the afternoon on the 17th of April, 1993, they surrendered; is that correct, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The 4th Battalion of the ABiH, or most of them, up to 90 soldiers, surrendered. I don't know where the others went, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at paragraph 77 now. It says that on the 17th to 18th of April, the HVO collected and detained approximately 70 to 90 military-aged Bosnian Muslim men at a school in Sovici. General, are these the members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their commander signed for their surrender, Mr. Ovnovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This report further states that the HVO forces killed at least four Bosnian Muslims near the Sovici school, and the HVO soldiers also beat, mistreated, and abused other men. General, in the Main Staff did you receive a report on such treatment meted out by HVO members towards ABiH members?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't receive such report. We received information according to which about seven members of the ABiH had been killed, two were wounded, one of which was moved to the HVO hospital in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at paragraph 78 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then that will be the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll then conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, so I just have one final question in that case, General. My colleague Scott -- Mr. Scott completed his cross-examination by claiming that you participated or you were one of the participants -- you failed to process and punish HVO soldiers who had committed crimes in the area of Herceg-Bosna. My final question, General, is as follows: In your opinion, in fact, in Herceg-Bosna, who strove the most to solve the conflict with the Muslims through negotiations, through agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was the one who did that. I met with them on the most numerous occasions, spoke to them, and negotiated with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We saw an interview you gave for "Srna" in which you said that it is better to negotiate for two years instead of to spend one day waging war. General, tell me, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my position, because when I saw what could be done in wartime, naturally it's better to discuss matters and to allow everything to be solved on a political level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more time. Thank you for the additional time you granted me. With your leave, I would like to thank the interpreters, all the interpreters, for their co-operation, and I apologise for driving a little too fast on occasion. I would, in particular, like to apologise to the English booth. If we sometimes had comments about the interpretation and failed to make these comments with tact, that really wasn't our intention. We just want to do have a faithful transcript. And thank you, and I do apologise if we have offended them. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to intervene with regard to the transcript. On page 35, line 20, it says that General Petkovic said: [In English] "About seven members of the ABiH had been killed."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard him saying about seven members of the ABiH were killed in combat, two were wounded, and one was moved to the HVO hospital. That's what it says. They weren't killed; they died in combat. That was how it was put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they died in combat. To conclude, Your Honours, I just have half a minute. Yesterday, my counsel asked me about a meeting with Susak, and forgot to mention a date, and I would like to mention it now. In December 1993, at the invitation of Minister Jukic, General Roso, the HVO discussed about how to reorganise the Guards Brigades, and at a meeting, at that discussion Mr. Susak was present with two or three Croatian Army officers. They were to give instructions as to how we should organise the Guards Brigades, because we had no experience. So as to my meeting with Mr. Susak, well, that's what I would like to add, what happened in December 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's in the transcript now. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning to each of Your Honours. Good morning to counsel, good morning to all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honours, before we break, and just to close out the record, so to speak, on Mr. Petkovic's testimony, it seemed to us, in further reflecting on wrapping things up on this, that as to the various tables that the Prosecution submitted, that for the purposes of the record they should be at least identified -- if nothing else, identified, because they were used fairly extensively at some places. We would ask to give an IC list to each of the tables. And we've raised this with the Registry, and perhaps the easiest way for me to do this is to give the title of our tables, and the Registry can assist us by assigning an IC number. And then I have one other very brief matter to raise. If we could just do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first table that we tendered -- well, not tendered, my apologies, we used with the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Before you start enumerating this, could we just express our position? The Petkovic Defence, Your Honours, is against this request, because so far the rule has been that IC numbers should be given only for documents with regard to which a witness has made certain comments. My colleague Mr. Scott wants IC numbers for documents that he compiled, and they are a compilation of a number of documents, and this would then fail to comply with the obligation that for documents that aren't exhibits, in accordance with your rules, he should show why there is a good reason to use those documents now, although he didn't use them before, although they aren't 65 ter list documents. If IC numbers are given to these documents, to these documents compiled, which weren't commented by Mr. Petkovic, I think this would be contrary to the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we won't start a discussion about that now. Given your documents -- your documents, your charts, you can list them on a document, and then in conformity with our guide-lines, ask for them to be admitted. The Defence will then object or will refer to page 34 for its objection, and then the Chamber will rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I do appreciate that. And it sounds to me, at least, if I can be bold enough to say, I think the Chamber and the Prosecution, at least in this respect, are on the same page. I think my good friend Ms. Alaburic has jumped the gun, as often happens. We haven't tendered them into admission yet, but there is a basic practice of identify matters that have been used in the courtroom. And if I compare this to the number of maps and other items Mr. Praljak has had -- among others, has had marked in the courtroom, I don't see any distinction whatsoever. If the Prosecution tenders them into admission, if we do, then, of course, there will be a separate phase in which those issues can be raised. So for purposes that they are in the record, so to speak, and they are identified, we used a title -- table titled "Herceg-Bosna and the HVO," and I would ask for an IC number to be provided to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll confer with my colleague. You agree? Yes, the Chamber agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you want to do them, Mr. Registry [sic], one by one, or -- either way is easiest for you. We have: "The HV Croatian Army in Bosnia and Herzegovina"; "Serb-Croat Co-operation"; "HVO-Serb Co-operation in Vares"; "Forced Labour"; "Military Discipline and Justice." There should be one more. There should be one more, Your Honour, I'm sorry, the one we used at the end of the day yesterday. Sorry, Your Honour, there's one stapled together. My fault. And then there was one called "HVO Enforcement Actions." Those are the tables we used, Your Honour. We would also tender, as a group -- sorry, strike the word "tender." We would also ask to identify as a group, again for purposes of being identified in the record, the actual slides that we used with the witness which we would tender as a group. And in the interests of time, I can provide those particular slide numbers to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a collective number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For each of the documents just mentioned by the Prosecutor, I shall give IC01195, 01196, 01197, 01198, 01199, 011200 [sic], and for the consolidated slides, I shall give it IC01201. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Small correction. 01200 will be the last one, not 011200.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the final item and I know it's getting a bit past the normal break time, but then we can hopefully start -- finish -- start clean after the break. The Chamber will recall, perhaps, that with some of these more extensive witnesses, I think its been a practice and we would certainly ask that we have a little bit of additional time to provide the IC list, and this would apply to all parties, not just the Prosecution, in terms of the documents actually being tendered. I spoke about this with Ms. Alaburic a couple of days ago. It was an agreement that all the parties could tender their IC lists for Mr. Petkovic not later than next Wednesday, if that would be agreeable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, we will now have our break. You will now return to your former place that is to my right, and then we will be calling the Coric Defence witness. So we will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Ms. Alaburic, you have no more witnesses. As we are living in a certain formalism, it is necessary to say, for the benefit of the transcript, that you have no more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not have any further witnesses. We have completed our case with the testimony of General Petkovic. We assume that nothing out of the ordinary will happen in the meantime. We do not intend to appeal for certification of witness statements under 92 bis. We do, indeed, intend to file a request for documentary evidence. And could you give us a dead-line that would be until the end of this month of this year, if possible, for the filing of this motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, will you stand, please. Could you tell us your first and last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Miroslav Desnica. I was born on the 10th of December, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm currently unemployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in a court of law on the events that took place in ex-Yugoslavia or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time for me to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may be seated. I wish to bid you good day once again. Let me give you some information. You are going to answer questions that will be put to you by the counsel for Mr. Coric. After that, Mr. Kovacic may have some questions for you. I don't know; this is possible. It's also possible for the other counsel to have questions for you. After that, the Prosecutor will have an hour to ask you questions. The Judges before you may also ask you questions. As we have a very tight agenda, if everything evolves normally and there are no problems linked to objections, your testimony may be completed today. Should there be problems and objections, then it is possible that we will continue with your testimony on Monday. That is what I wanted to say, hoping that everything will evolve as planned. Without further adieu, I give the floor to Defence counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. Good day, Mr. Desnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I have already spoken to Mr. Scott about this and they don't mind, I would like, as an introduction, to put a leading question to you linked to your curriculum vitae, if I get permission from the Chamber so as to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Desnica, is it true from 1972 until 1976, you attended a secondary school in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out the places that you were in so that you will answer all of these questions at once. Is it true that from 1976 until 1980, you attended and completed the Naval Military Academy in Split?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, until 1990, you were a member of the Yugoslav Navy, from which you left with the role of lieutenant of a military vessel in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that from 1990 until 1991, you were a teacher in the Naval Centre in Split, teaching the subject of special equipment and armaments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that from 1991 until 1997, you were employed in the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, the Police Administration for Split and Dalmatia, the Department for Defence Affairs, with the title of independent inspector?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also right that in 1997, you left the MUP of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's all. Mr. Desnica, will you please look at the documents? Could we have the assistance of the usher? Could he give the witness the documents, please? Mr. Desnica, would you look at the first document in the binder. That is document PD05109 [as interpreted] -- 5D5109. Tell me, is this your statement, Mr. Desnica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read this statement in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you stand by everything you said in the statement or do you wish to change or add anything to it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: I wish to stand by this statement in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: If you were to testify once again about the facts that you testified to in your statement, would your testimony be the same to what is contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Yes, my statement would be absolutely the same as that contained in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Desnica. Now let us have a look at a few more documents. Will you please -- to remind you, you have your statement in front of you, and in paragraph 8 of that statement you mention the literature that you used in the training process. So in that connection, I'd like us to look at a few documents. The first is PD05113 [as interpreted] -- 5D0 -- 5D5113. Tell me, please, Mr. Desnica, what kind of document is this, and are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: It is a textbook for police officer, and it's entitled "Command and Combat Tactics in the Police."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen paragraph 8 of your statement, so look at the pages and paragraphs linked to the training. What could you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: This document -- or, rather, these paragraphs discuss the use of police forces in peacetime and exceptional conditions, that is, in possible wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Look now at document PD0 -- 5D -- 5D05114, and tell me, again, what kind of a document this is.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: This is also a handbook for the training of policemen, and it deals with subjects linked to the lawfulness of the activities of the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: The next document, please, 5D05115. The same question again. What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: It is the Law on Internal Affairs or the Constitutional Law of the Republic of Croatia, and the main thesis or the main topic is linked to humaneness, that is, the principles underlying the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 from the beginning, you have a section relating to human rights and freedoms. In your statement, you said that you used this in training. Why did you use this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
utterances.text: Because we sought to underline, through the Constitutional Law as the fundamental law of any state, though this was in another state, but this is an example from our own state, linked to the human rights and freedoms, which are the fundamental principles of such a law, based on international conventions on the protection of human rights, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me caution you. You have to slow down a little. You're speaking too fast. Look now at the document 2D00751. And tell me what you know about this document, but slowly, please, very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DESNICA
